teachingPlaylist.title: Observe & Understand — Run the baseline program
teachingPlaylist.description: Compile and run the provided program; see heap allocation via a pointer and how user input becomes elements of the dynamically allocated array.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Identify where memory is allocated, how the pointer is used as an array, and where memory is freed.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: We're going to compile the starter file: say gcc main dot c dash o grades. Run it and enter three as the count, then 80, 90, 70. Watch prompts and the final printed average. Notice how grades was declared as float star and used with bracket notation. Pause and explain where each input was stored and why free is called at the end.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Input sequence: 3 then 80, 90, 70. Expected output: Average grade: 80.00. This shows sum/num_grades behavior.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You have a simple CLI program that must store a variable number of floats determined by the user at runtime.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Run the program with the sample inputs and say aloud where each grade is stored in memory.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Entering 0 or a negative number — the program should detect this and exit with a friendly message.
teachingPlaylist.recap: You saw dynamic allocation with malloc/calloc and learned that pointers can be used like arrays. Freeing memory returns it to the heap.
codeSteps: Observe the average printed and the prompts.

teachingPlaylist.title: Modify & Experiment — Swap malloc for calloc
teachingPlaylist.description: Make a one-line change replacing malloc with calloc to explore zero-initialized heap memory.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Understand the difference between malloc (uninitialized) and calloc (zero-initialized) and how initialization can prevent reading garbage.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Open the allocation line and replace malloc with calloc, using two arguments: the number of elements and the size of each element. Recompile and run with the same test inputs to confirm behavior. Think about situations where zero-initialized memory reduces bugs.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Change line: grades = (float *) calloc(num_grades, sizeof(float)); Recompile and rerun the program: expected average remains 80.00 for the sample inputs.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You are debugging a program that sometimes reads zeros unexpectedly — calloc could help if you need initial zeros.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Make the change, compile, and run the sample. Then explain whether you observed any different behavior and why.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Using calloc but relying on old uninitialized values elsewhere — remember that calloc only zeroes newly allocated bytes.
teachingPlaylist.recap: calloc is helpful for defaulting memory to zero. The program should still read inputs and compute the average correctly.
codeSteps: Open main.c and find the allocation line.
Replace malloc(num_grades * sizeof(float)) with calloc(num_grades, sizeof(float)).
Save and compile: gcc main.c -o grades
Run sample input and confirm output.

teachingPlaylist.title: Build & Integrate — Add realloc-based resizing
teachingPlaylist.description: Add a short interaction to allow the user to change the requested size, and expand the grades array with realloc. Use a temporary pointer and handle failure safely.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Learn safe realloc usage and how to expand an existing heap allocation without losing data or leaking memory.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: After the first allocation, ask the user for a new total. If they pick a different total, call realloc and assign its result to a temporary pointer. If tmp is NULL, keep the original allocation and inform the user. If tmp is non-NULL, update grades to tmp and adjust the total. Then read that many grades and compute the average.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Sample run: initial 2, change to 4, grades 70, 80, 90, 100 -> Average grade: 85.00.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: Users sometimes change their mind about how much data they'll enter — support dynamic resizing safely at runtime.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Implement the realloc pattern, compile, then run the sample. If realloc fails, what does the program do?
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Directly assigning realloc return to the original pointer without checking for NULL — this can cause a memory leak if realloc fails.
teachingPlaylist.recap: Always use a temporary pointer with realloc. If success, replace original pointer; if failure, keep original and handle gracefully.
codeSteps: Insert prompt asking for a new total after allocation.
Call realloc and store result in a temporary pointer.
Check tmp for NULL before assigning to grades.
If expanded, initialize the new slots to 0.0f for safety.
Compile and run the sample inputs to verify average computation.

teachingPlaylist.title: Verify & Extend — Test edge cases and plan median extension
teachingPlaylist.description: Run edge-case tests, verify validation, and design an extension to compute median using qsort.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Confirm robust behavior for invalid input; prepare for a realistic extension that requires sorting and pointer-based manipulation.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Test invalid counts (0 or negative) and small counts. Observe the defensive messages. For extension, outline how you'd compute the median: call qsort with a comparator for float values, then pick the middle element or average two middle elements. This solidifies your understanding of array access via pointers and in-place operations.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample:
Run: printf "0
" | ./grades -> program prints Number of grades must be positive. Run: printf "1
100
" | ./grades -> prints Average grade: 100.00.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: Before shipping, run edge-case tests so your program doesn't crash on bad input; plan next feature (median).
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Run the edge-case tests, then write a two-line plan for computing median using qsort.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Attempting to compute median without sorting first; median requires elements ordered by value.
teachingPlaylist.recap: Validation prevents bad allocations. Sorting in place + qsort lets you compute median without extra heap allocations.
codeSteps: Run: printf "0\n" | ./grades and confirm validation message.
Write a short plan to compute a median using qsort and in-place selection.

tasks.title: Scene 1 — Observe & Understand: Run the baseline program
tasks.narratorGuide: Goal: see the baseline behavior of the provided program. First, compile the starter file and run it. When I say compile, I mean run gcc space main dot c space dash o space grades. The program asks "How many grades do you want to enter?" — that's where you type a small integer like three and press Enter. Then type three floats like 80, 90, 70 when prompted. Watch the prompts carefully: each "Enter grade" comes from the loop that writes into the heap memory pointed to by grades. Finally, you'll see the Average grade printed. Pause and describe aloud: what did the pointer variable store? Where did your inputs go? Good observation — you're ready to try a small change.

tasks.title: Scene 2 — Modify & Experiment: Replace malloc with calloc (1-2 line change)
tasks.narratorGuide: Connect: calloc stands for contiguous allocation and zero-initializes the block. Observe: change the single allocation line from malloc to calloc. To do this, open main.c and replace malloc(num_grades * sizeof(float)) with calloc(num_grades, sizeof(float)). Save and recompile. Test: run the same inputs as before. You should still get Average grade: 80.00 for the sample inputs. Explain: calloc helps avoid uninitialized memory by giving you zeros — useful when you want default values. Pause: say out loud why calloc might help avoid bugs in programs that depend on default-initialized memory.

tasks.title: Scene 3 — Build & Integrate: Allow resizing with realloc
tasks.narratorGuide: Connect: realloc resizes a previously allocated block. We'll add a brief interaction: after allocating for the initial number, ask the user if they want to increase the number of grades. If they do, call realloc. Important safety pattern: store realloc's return in a temporary pointer, check for NULL, and only overwrite the original pointer on success. Implement this and compile. Test: run the program with an initial size of 2, then enter 4 as the new total, then provide four grades: 70, 80, 90, 100. The program should print Average grade: 85.00. Explain verbally why using a temporary pointer prevents losing the original allocation on realloc failure.

tasks.title: Scene 4 — Verify & Extend: Test edge cases and plan an extension
tasks.narratorGuide: Connect: validation prevents invalid allocation sizes. Verify: run the program with 0 or negative input and watch the error. Experiment: enter a very small number and then a very large number? Note system limits. Extend: plan how you would compute the median: you would need to sort the grades array (for example with qsort) and then pick the middle element (or average the middle two). That requires no extra heap allocation if you sort in place. Pause: write down your plan for implementing median in two steps: sort in place, then compute median depending on parity.

checks.explanation: Program must read three grades and print the correct average.
Basic validation must reject non-positive counts.
After replacing malloc with calloc the program should still accept input and compute the correct average.
Confirm the code uses calloc with two parameters.
Program should accept an initial size, allow resizing to 4, accept four grades and compute the correct average.
If the user reduces the number, the program should still read the final count and compute average without crashing.
Confirm realloc call and temporary pointer use are present in the source.
Program must refuse non-positive counts and exit with a message.
Final check (manual): create a short implementation plan to compute the median using qsort on the grades array.
